summary: Defines how to compress CoAP headers using the Static Context Header Compression and fragmentation framework. SCHC uses a static description of header fields to reduce redundancy and size, which suits constrained devices.

eli5.summary: Both sides share a codebook so they can send short codes instead of long messages.

what is a compression residue in schc
how does schc work with oscore
subtitle: How to shrink CoAP headers with SCHC rules so constrained devices can use them over low-power wide-area networks.

tldr.problem: A CoAP header is still too large for LPWANs (Low-Power Wide-Area Networks), and CoAP differs from IPv6 and UDP because its header is flexible and asymmetric between requests and responses.
tldr.mechanism: SCHC Rules list each CoAP field with a target value, a matching operator and a compression action, and use the direction indicator to treat requests and responses differently. Options and OSCORE-protected messages get their own guidance.
tldr.outcome: Fields that are predictable can be left out entirely and only a RuleID plus a small Compression Residue is sent. With OSCORE the worked example costs about 10 bytes more than without it.

today: RFC 8824 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2021, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the SCHC framework of RFC 8724.

sections.title: SCHC Applied to CoAP
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252) is a command and response protocol for microcontrollers with small RAM and ROM. Even so, its header is too large for LPWANs. RFC 8724 defines the SCHC framework, which compresses headers using a static context that both endpoints know before transmission. How the context is provisioned is out of scope here.

A context holds Rules. A Rule is an ordered list of Field Descriptors, each with a Field ID (FID), Field Length (FL), Field Position (FP), Direction Indicator (DI) and Target Value (TV). A Matching Operator (MO) decides whether the field fits, and a Compression/Decompression Action (CDA) says how to compress it. If a Rule matches, the matched fields are replaced by a RuleID and a Compression Residue holding the leftover bits.

This RFC adds no new mechanism. It says how to apply the framework to CoAP headers. If no Rule matches, the packet MUST be sent uncompressed using the RuleID reserved for that purpose.
sections.eli5: A rule is a recipe card both sides already have. If a message fits a card, you only send the card number and any bits that vary.

sections.title: Where Compression Happens
sections.content:
SCHC compression of CoAP MAY be done together with the lower layers (IPv6 and UDP) or independently. The RFC shows three arrangements.

  • At the LPWAN boundary: one Rule compresses the whole stack from IPv6 to CoAP, and the Device and the Network Gateway (NGW) perform compression and decompression. The application does not need SCHC.
  • Standalone, end to end: SCHC runs in the CoAP layer. The RuleID, Compression Residue and payload are encrypted, for example with DTLS, so only the other end can read them. This needs an end-to-end context between Device and application.
  • With OSCORE: two Rules are needed, one for the Inner header and one for the Outer header that includes the OSCORE options.

When several SCHC instances are involved, their Rules may come from different provisioning domains.
sections.eli5: You can shrink the message at the gateway on the way out, or shrink it yourself and lock it in a box so only the final receiver can open it.

sections.title: How CoAP Differs from IPv6 and UDP
sections.content:
CoAP is harder to compress than IPv6 and UDP for several reasons.

  • Asymmetry. Requests and responses carry different headers. A Uri-Path is mandatory in a request and may be absent in the response. The DI lets a single Rule treat each direction differently.
  • Different values per direction. A client that sends only Confirmable (CON) requests can have its Type elided, and the answer needs one bit to say ACK or RST. The Code field splits into the 0.0X request format and the Y.ZZ response format.
  • Variable lengths. IPv6 and UDP fields have fixed sizes, but some CoAP fields vary, and options use Type-Length-Value encoding. A Rule can set the Field Length to variable, and then SCHC sends the length in the Compression Residue.
  • Repeated fields. URI path and query elements can occur several times, so the Field Position tells instances apart.
  • Fields too long for LPWAN. Message ID and Token can be compressed with the Most Significant Bits (MSB) MO.
sections.eli5: Compressing IP is like packing identical boxes. CoAP is like packing odd-shaped items that change between trips there and back, so the packing list needs more detail.

sections.title: Compressing Header Fields and Options
sections.content:
For the fixed header, the Version MUST be elided because it always holds the same value. The Type SHOULD be elided if a client sends only NON or only CON messages, otherwise a match-mapping MO can be used. The Code follows the same idea and can be split into request and response descriptors using the DI. The Message ID can use the MSB MO with the LSB CDA.

The Token has two parts. Token Length is treated like any field. For Token Value, SCHC MUST NOT send it as variable-length data, to avoid ambiguity, so the Rule MUST use the function tkl, which returns the value in the Token Length field.

Options use the Delta-Type, Length, Value format. The FID carries the option number, and the TV the option value. Request and response options differ, so Rules can tag the DI. If CoAP adds a new option, Rules MAY be updated, and until a Rule exists the header goes uncompressed.

  • Content, Accept, Max-Age, Uri-Host and Uri-Port can be elided if known, mapped if from a small set, or sent as values.
  • Uri-Path and Uri-Query repeat, so FP distinguishes them. The Field Length MUST be variable, and MSB sizes MUST be a multiple of 8 bits. For a variable number of elements, create several Rules or one Rule with entries for the longest path.
  • ETag, If-Match, If-None-Match, Location-Path and Location-Query cannot be stored in a Rule, so their values MUST always be sent in the Compression Residue.
sections.eli5: Things that never change are skipped. Things that come from a short menu are sent as a menu number. Things that can be anything are simply sent in full.

sections.title: Extensions and OSCORE
sections.content:
Several CoAP extensions get specific treatment. A Block option (RFC 7959) MUST be sent in the Compression Residue, using an empty TV, MO ignore and CDA value-sent. CoAP block-wise transfer and SCHC fragmentation are complementary and may both be used on a packet. The Observe option (RFC 7641) is sent as a value with a maximum size of 3 bytes, and a specific Rule SHOULD exist for the RST message that cancels observation. The No-Response option (RFC 7967) can be elided with equal and not-sent if both ends know its value.

OSCORE (RFC 8613) provides end-to-end protection. Its option value starts with a flag byte whose top three bits are zero, then bits h (kid context present), k (kid present) and a 3-bit n giving the length of the Partial IV. The Rule splits the option into four Field Descriptors: OSCORE_flags, OSCORE_piv, OSCORE_kidctx and OSCORE_kid.

OSCORE splits a message into an Outer header and an encrypted Inner Plaintext. SCHC compresses both stages independently, with Inner Rules before encryption and Outer Rules after it. Because the Inner part is decrypted only at the end, the receiving endpoint must also implement Inner SCHC compression and decompression.
sections.eli5: For secret messages there are two wrappers. You shrink the inside message, lock it, and then shrink the outer label that goes with it.

sections.title: Worked Examples and the Cost of Security
sections.content:
The first example is a mandatory header with a CON message. The Rule elides the version and Token Length, shrinks the 25 method and response codes to 5 bits using match-mapping, and sends only the Type, a mapped code and 9 bits of the Message ID. A client in an application server may not match that Rule if the Message ID does not start with 7 zero bits, but a CoAP proxy before the SCHC compressor can rewrite the Message ID to fit.

The OSCORE example uses a GET request for temperature and its Content response. The original messages are 17 bytes and 10 bytes. With OSCORE and SCHC the compressed request is 12 bytes and the response 16 bytes. Compressed with SCHC but without OSCORE, they are 2 bytes and 6 bytes. The authentication tag is fixed in length and cannot be compressed, so this is the cost of integrity protection. The RFC sums it up as a difference of about 10 bytes.
sections.eli5: Locking a message in a box makes it a bit bigger, because the lock itself cannot be squeezed. In the example the locked version is about 10 bytes bigger.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SCHC compression changes only how header information is represented. It does not raise or lower the security of the communication. If no security protocol such as OSCORE or DTLS is used, a Layer 2 security mechanism is needed. For a Layer 2 other than an LPWAN, cryptographic integrity protection of the SCHC headers is REQUIRED.

With OSCORE Outer headers, the IV size in the Compression Residue involves a trade-off: a longer MSB prefix compresses better but the Device must renew key material more often, which takes several message exchanges and energy-intensive computation. Compressor and decompressor Rules MUST stay in sync, so any time Rules are updated on an OSCORE endpoint, it MUST trigger OSCORE key re-establishment.

A corrupted compressed packet could cause denial of service through resource use at the decompressor, though an attacker able to inject packets on the link could do more damage. A wrong length in a variable-length Compression Residue is detected and the packet is dropped. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Shrinking a message does not make it safer or less safe. If you want it secret, you still need a lock, and both sides must keep their codebooks matching.
